claim: Legal CBR compares a new case to precedents through factors (fact patterns) and a small set of argument moves (analogise, distinguish, downplay, emphasise, cite counterexample), not raw similarity.
agent_test: Prompt with explicit analogise/distinguish moves vs plain 'find a similar case' at equal tokens on a precedent task.

claim: In the surveys and design papers read (Rissland, Ashley and Branting 2006; Bench-Capon 1997, 1999, 2012), factor-based symbolic legal CBR is illustrated mostly by worked examples, with one small blind expert-graded comparison (GREBE vs law students) and no quantitative accuracy reported.
agent_test: Do not borrow claimed gains; measure our own.
audit_note: The opened surveys and design papers (Rissland et al. 2006, Bench-Capon 1997) do show worked examples and one blind expert-graded test (GREBE) and no accuracy figures, but the sources are only a survey and design papers, and factor-based systems such as IBP were evaluated quantitatively elsewhere, so the field-wide claim is wider than the sources.
claim_before_audit: Factor-based symbolic CBR was validated mostly by worked examples and small expert-graded tests; surveys and design papers report almost no quantitative accuracy.

claim: Frontier LLMs reliably find distinctions between two cases when factors are given (100% on Task 1, 253 instances, all 6 models).
agent_test: Re-run Task 1 on our agent with raw text instead of given factors.

claim: Hierarchical argumentative support is harder (Task 2: 64.82% to 92.09%) and identifying significant distinctions collapses (Task 3: 11.46% to 33.99%, most under 25%). Verified in paper text.
agent_test: Run Task 3 pairs through our scaffold vs plain CoT at equal tokens.

claim: Thinking mode helps much on legal analogical tasks: Qwen3-235B 78.66% vs 30.04% non-thinking on Task 2, 33.99% vs 0.00% on Task 3. Confounded with post-training.
agent_test: Compare thinking vs non-thinking of the same model at matched token budgets.

claim: More thinking tokens do not mean better answers: gpt-5 used 3,189 tokens for 92.09% while qwen3-thinking used 9,596 for 78.66%; wrong gpt-5 answers used 4,456 tokens vs 3,081 for correct (+45%).
agent_test: Test whether token length on an item predicts error and can trigger a re-check or stop.

claim: CATO factor information is linearly decodable in small open LLM hidden layers (best-layer AUC 0.86 to 1.00), but TF-IDF also does well and presence in activations is not use in reasoning. Gap check: authors state no intervention test was run and only synthetic text was used.
agent_test: Not testable at prompt level; low priority.

claim: LLMs given factor sets often fail to use all factors in prose arguments (utilization recall 42% to 85%) and rarely abstain on non-arguable cases (0% to 87%; 7 of 8 models below 60%).
agent_test: Add an explicit 'no arguable case' check and measure abstention rate on non-arguable inputs.

claim: LLMs hallucinate heavily recalling cases from memory: 58% (GPT-4) to 88% (Llama 2); at least 49% even on easy tasks; deciding whether two cases agree is near chance.
agent_test: Require retrieval of case text before citing; compare hallucinated-citation rate with and without.

claim: Commercial legal RAG tools still hallucinate (17% to 33%, 202 queries, opened) but less than closed-book GPT-4 (about 43%); retrieval alone does not make case reuse safe.
agent_test: Check each cited case against retrieved text as a verification step.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: In two recent studies, legal case retrieval stays hard: ReaKase-8B reaches micro-F1 28.7 on COLIEE 2023 (BM25 21.4) and a four-stage pipeline on an Indian prior-case task reaches 25.5, with lexical BM25 a strong baseline; in the latter, rankers with internal MRR up to 0.97 scored as low as 0.14 on the official evaluation, so internal validation can badly overstate performance.
agent_test: Compare lexical vs embedding vs reasoning-based retrieval for analogue memory.
audit_note: Two papers only: the best micro-F1 is 28.7 (ReaKase-8B, COLIEE 2022/23) and 25.5 (Sha et al., Indian legal documents, not COLIEE); the paper calls the internal-vs-official gap (MRR 0.97 vs 0.14) a validation mismatch, not leakage.
claim_before_audit: Case retrieval is hard: best COLIEE-type micro-F1 stays below 30%, BM25 is a strong baseline, and internal-vs-official gaps (MRR 0.97 vs 0.14) show leakage risk.

claim: Case-based RAG gives a small gain over a strong no-retrieval baseline (+1.94% cosine, 0.8967 to 0.9141); metric is weak and weights were tuned on the same data.
agent_test: Repeat with a correctness metric, not embedding cosine.

claim: Case memory for general agents helps modestly: Memento adds 4.7 to 9.6 points out of distribution; the first retrieved case gives most of the gain (K=0 59.9 F1, K=4 64.5, K=32 63.9); ExpeL retrieval and insights both help.
agent_test: Sweep K=0,1,4,8 retrieved cases at equal token cost.

claim: Distilled lessons beat raw case retrieval on some tasks (ExpeL HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, opened) and lose on others (ALFWorld 50% vs 55%; WebShop 37% vs 38%): task type decides.
agent_test: Compare raw cases vs distilled rules in memory per task type.

claim: Precedent as context improves legal judgment prediction in one Chinese-law study, but the ablation label was inferred from a garbled table.
agent_test: Verify before use.

claim: LLM judges are persuadable: advocate quality shifts outcomes by 8% to 21% and stronger advocates win 58% to 71%; a risk for any agent weighing arguments for and against.
agent_test: Test whether a presented opposing view changes our agent's answer on fixed-answer items.

claim: Formal accounts of precedential constraint (reason model vs result model) disagree and no empirical test chooses between them.
agent_test: None; theory.

claim: LLM annotation of legal text is mediocre: GPT-4 reached F1 .51 to .57 classifying court-opinion sentences by their value for interpreting a statutory concept (Savelka et al. 2023), and annotating drug-stop cases with canonical factors gave MCC 0.32 (gpt-4o) to 0.52 (llama) with ElasticNet (Gray et al. 2024); human-refined factors beat fully LLM-refined ones but did not reliably beat canonical factors.
agent_test: Test factor extraction from raw text as first scaffold step vs direct comparison.
audit_note: Savelka et al. F1 .51-.57 is for classifying sentences by value for interpreting a statutory concept (not legal factors), and in Gray et al. human-refined factors did not reliably beat canonical ones for LLM annotation (llama 0.56 vs 0.52 ElasticNet but 0.46 vs 0.61 RF; gpt-4o 0.30 vs 0.32); they only beat LLM-refined factors.
claim_before_audit: LLM annotation of legal factors from text is mediocre: F1 .51 to .57 (GPT-4, 2023) and MCC 0.32 to 0.52 with canonical factors; human-refined factors help.

claim: Rule induction from analogous cases is weak with direct prompting: implicit-rule recall about 25% to 48%, micro-F1 46.9 to 66.7.
agent_test: Compare an abstract-a-rule step vs direct answer.

claim: IBP near-91% accuracy on 186 cases and CATO instructor parity are recalled, not verified.
agent_test: Open the originals before any citation.

claim: Commercial legal RAG tools (Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, Ask Practical Law AI) hallucinate 17% to 33% of the time versus about 43% for closed-book GPT-4 (a relative cut of roughly 23% to 60%), so retrieval reduces but does not remove errors; the dangerous residue is a real case cited for a holding it does not contain (misgrounding).
agent_test: Grade each citation on correct holding AND source support, with and without a read-the-text step, equal tokens.
audit_note: Going from about 43% (GPT-4 closed-book) to 17-33% is a relative cut of about 23% to 60%, not 'a third to a half'; the tools are commercial legal RAG products, not generic retrieval.
claim_before_audit: Retrieving case or statute text first cuts false or misgrounded answers by about a third to a half against closed-book (about 43% to 17-33%) but leaves a floor; the dangerous residue is a real case cited for a holding it lacks.

claim: No study found tests a forced steelman against sycophancy to cited authority. The one full-text legal sycophancy study (EU law, 1,127 items) tests no mitigation, and finds larger reasoning models defer more to misleading context (POI 43.1% vs 78.2%).
agent_test: Plant a false authority; compare plain, steelman-the-other-side and verify-source conditions.

claim: Within one question, shorter reasoning samples are more often correct than longer ones (up to 34.5 points over the longest), and wrong gpt-5 legal answers used 45% more tokens; this supports a relative length trigger for re-check, not an absolute cap, because hard questions need longer chains.
agent_test: Sample k answers; if the chosen one is far longer than the others, force a re-check. Measure gain at equal tokens.
audit_note: The 45% extra tokens for wrong gpt-5 answers is for legal Task 2 only (4,456 vs 3,081); the 'relative trigger, not absolute cap' conclusion is the researcher's inference.

claim: In ExpeL, relevance of retrieved cases is the main lever (ALFWorld 59.0 task-similar vs 42.5 random vs 40.0 no cases) and model-written insights beat hand-written ones (HotpotQA 39.0 vs 32.0), but reflections added to insight writing hurt (29.0).
agent_test: Test random vs similar analogues in the agent memory.

claim: Self-generated analogues help strong models over zero-shot CoT (GSM8K 61% vs 50%, text-davinci-003) and beat retrieved ones, but lose at weak scale; 3 to 5 exemplars is the sweet spot and 1 is worse.
agent_test: Use model-recalled analogues on strong models only; retrieve real cases for weak models.

claim: Prompts naming legal reasoning steps lifted GPT-3 on statute entailment (+15.79% over the COLIEE 2021 winner with the best prompt) but no study found tests analogise/distinguish moves against plain similarity on case pairs with chat LLMs.
agent_test: Run plain-similarity vs analogise/distinguish prompts on HYPO-style case pairs.

claim: Decodable factor structure has not been tested causally: the authors of the probing paper list intervention (suppress or amplify features) as future work, and evaluate only generated trade-secret narratives.
agent_test: Do not claim the model uses factors it can decode.

claim: Best K for legal retrieval is a trade-off: recall climbs and precision falls from k=1 to 64 (PrivacyQA P@1 14.38%, R@64 84.19%; MAUD 2.65% and 28.28%); retrieval metrics do not give the best K for reasoning, which agent evidence puts at a few cases (about 3 to 5).
agent_test: Sweep K = 1, 3, 5, 10 on answer correctness.

claim: An apparently non-Pittsburgh group (LePREC) extracts factors with an LLM and scores them with a sparse linear model on 769 real Malaysian contract cases, reporting 30-40% over GPT-4o (62% precision); abstract-level only and a different task, so not a replication of the factor benchmarks.
agent_test: Read the full paper before use.
